title: Segmentation: bank-level partial-good DRAM sold as fractional-capacity SKUs
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation resolves 'bigger die vs. higher yield': each 16-32 Gb die is fused into independently testable 2 Gb bank-segments; dies with dead segments are not scrapped but shipped as 12/24 Gb parts whose map is burned into an SPD-like fuse block and honoured by the memory controller.
why: Yield loss and test scrap: recovers ~5-10% of wafer output as sellable bits with zero added fab capacity.

title: Taking out: move DRAM periphery to foundry wafers, hybrid-bond back
idea: TRIZ #2 Extraction: strip sense amps, decoders and I/O off the DRAM wafer so the scarce DRAM fab prints only cell arrays, while plentiful logic foundries build the periphery wafer; the two are joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding at 1-2 um pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die: ~1.6-1.9x more bits per scarce DRAM wafer start, and periphery gets faster logic transistors.

title: Local quality: lifetime-matched retention binning for short-lived AI data
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: instead of one 64 ms retention spec, bin dies by measured retention (8/16/32/64 ms) and sell fast-leaking dies into streaming buffers, activation scratchpads and NIC queues where data is overwritten before it decays; the controller refresh rate is read from the die's bin fuse.
why: Retention tail (fact 3) currently scraps or downgrades dies; matching data lifetime to retention adds ~3-6% sellable output.

title: Asymmetry: hyperscaler capex prepay for capped-price capacity call options
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry in risk-sharing: hyperscalers prepay ~30% of a new fab's capex and in return hold call options on 50% of its output at a capped price for 10 years, while the maker keeps all upside on the other half and all downside protection on the first.
why: Capital intensity and 3-5 year fab lag: de-risks greenfield builds so they start 1-2 years earlier during shortages.

title: Merging: regional memory utility selling pooled DRAM as GB-hours
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: a utility operator owns rack-scale CXL-switched DRAM pools in colocation hubs and leases capacity per GB-hour to many tenants, merging the stranded headroom each server is provisioned with into one shared pool.
why: Stranded DRAM is ~25-30% of installed server memory; pooling frees that much supply without making a single new bit.

title: Universality: one universal die with fuse-selected DDR5/LPDDR/HBM-core personality
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: design a single array die whose PHY, burst logic and TSV landing pads support DDR5, LPDDR5X and HBM-core roles, chosen by fuses after wafer sort, so fabs never commit wafers to the wrong product months before demand is known.
why: Product-mix misallocation and inventory whiplash: ~5-10% effective supply gain plus faster response to price spikes.

title: Nesting: fab-in-fab DRAM lines inside idle logic, solar and LED shells
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: insert a compact 10-20k wspm DRAM module line into existing idle cleanroom bays (shuttered 300 mm logic, solar-cell, LED or MEMS fabs) reusing their utilities, gas yards and permits.
why: Capital and time: cuts greenfield cost ~30-40% and time-to-wafer by ~2 years; boosts U.S. manufacturability.

title: Anti-weight: DRAM fab financed as regulated 30-year infrastructure asset
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: counter the crushing depreciation weight by financing fab shells and long-life tools through pension/sovereign infrastructure bonds at ~4% over 30 years with a regulated return, leaving only short-life tools on the maker's balance sheet.
why: Depreciation ~55% of wafer cost: halving WACC on long-lived assets cuts cost per bit ~15-20%.

title: Preliminary anti-action: cold-crucible levitation Czochralski removes quartz crucible dependency
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: pre-empt the Spruce Pine chokepoint by growing DRAM-grade silicon in water-cooled segmented copper cold crucibles with induction-levitated melt (skull melting), so the melt never touches high-purity quartz.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes >80% single-source HPQ crucible exposure and also cuts oxygen contamination.

title: Preliminary action: pre-permitted state memory megasites with utilities pre-built
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: states pre-permit, pre-grade and pre-plumb fab-ready megasites (substations, reclaimed-water plants, bulk gas, helium recovery, rail) before any tenant signs, so a DRAM maker starts tool install in months, not years.
why: Time and capital: trims 12-18 months from fab schedule; raises U.S. share of DRAM output.

title: Beforehand cushioning: mandated closed-loop helium recovery in every memory fab
idea: TRIZ #11 Cushion in advance: retrofit wafer-backside cooling, leak-check and litho purge lines with capture, membrane purification and recompression loops reclaiming ~90-95% of helium on-site, with a 6-month buffer cylinder bank.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30%, offline): cuts net helium draw ~10-20x, insulating output from supply shocks.

title: Equipotentiality: cross-company fab tool-hour exchange for idle litho and etch
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: standardize wafer carriers, recipe formats and contamination certificates so idle DUV scanners and etchers in logic and foundry fabs can accept DRAM lots by the hour through a brokered exchange with escrowed IP protection.
why: Capital intensity: monetizes stranded tool capacity, adding DRAM wafer starts without buying tools.

title: Inversion: pure-play DRAM foundry with open PDK for fabless designers
idea: TRIZ #13 Inversion: instead of three IDMs designing and fabbing their own DRAM, a pure-play DRAM foundry publishes a cell/array PDK and accepts designs from fabless memory startups, hyperscalers and universities, like TSMC did for logic.
why: Industry structure: unlocks new entrants and specialized memories without each building a $15B fab.

title: Spheroidality: 1 mm spherical-silicon memory micro-fab processed inside tubes
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: drop-tower-grown 1 mm silicon spheres roll through sealed tubes for clean, deposit, expose (spherical-mirror litho) and etch, then are clustered into memory modules; no ingots, crucibles or ballroom cleanrooms.
why: Capital and crucible chokepoints: a tube-fab could cost ~1/10 per wafer-equivalent, though density per sphere is limited.

title: Dynamics: flex-fab with rail-mounted tool pods reconfiguring routes in weeks
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: tools sit in standardized mobile pods on floor rails with quick-connect utilities, and the AMHS route is software-defined, so a line can re-balance between HBM, DDR5 and LPDDR process variants in weeks as prices move.
why: Supply responsiveness: shrinks the mismatch between price signals and output from quarters to weeks.

title: Partial action: Lego-fab adding 2,500-wafer modules as demand appears
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: rather than one $15B mega-fab, build containerized prefab cleanroom modules each sized for ~2,500 wspm of a fixed mature DRAM flow, adding modules in 9-month increments.
why: Capital intensity and cycle risk: lowers entry ticket to ~$1-2B and avoids overbuild at cycle peaks.

title: Another dimension: 16-high stacks of depreciated legacy-node DRAM dies
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: keep fully depreciated 2x/1x nm fabs running and gain density vertically by thinning their dies and stacking 16-high with low-cost hybrid or staggered wire-bond packaging for capacity-tier modules.
why: Cost per bit: depreciated wafers are ~40-50% cheaper; stacking restores density without EUV.

title: Mechanical vibration: ultrasonic debonding harvests DRAM dies from retired modules
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: retired DIMMs and phone boards pass through cryogenic shock plus ultrasonic delamination that releases BGA packages without thermal stress; packages are re-balled, retested and rebinned for CXL memory expanders.
why: Reuse/recycling: tens of exabytes of DDR4 retire yearly; even 10% recovery adds meaningful capacity-tier supply.

title: Periodic action: staggered counter-cyclical capex rotation under antitrust safe harbor
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: replace synchronized boom-bust fab building with a published rotation where each maker adds capacity in assigned years, supervised under a government safe harbor and backed by offtake guarantees in its slot.
why: Pig-cycle volatility: smooths supply so 4x price spikes and loss years are both dampened.

title: Continuity: government buyer-of-last-resort keeps DRAM fabs at full utilization
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: during downturns a national memory reserve buys known-good die at cost-plus, keeping tools at 100% loading; the stored die (dry-nitrogen cabinets) are released into the market during shortages.
why: Capital efficiency: idle tools waste depreciation; continuous loading plus a strategic buffer flattens price spikes.

title: Skipping: open shared qualification lab cutting new-entrant DRAM qualification to months
idea: TRIZ #21 Rushing through: a neutral lab runs one public, JEDEC-plus qualification suite (retention, row hammer, burn-in, platform interop) whose results all major CPU/GPU vendors accept, so new suppliers skip 12-18 months of per-customer qualification.
why: Market entry barrier: lets new fabs' bits reach servers ~1 year sooner.

title: Blessing in disguise: failed HBM stacks rebinned as HBM-lite via TSV bypass
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: build redundant TSV bypass lanes in every core die so a 12-high stack with one or two dead layers is re-addressed and sold as an 8-high 'HBM-lite' instead of scrap.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30%: converts much of that loss into sellable capacity.

title: Feedback: field-to-fab telemetry loop relaxes over-conservative test guardbands
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: hyperscalers stream anonymized per-die correctable-error and retention telemetry back to the fab, which uses it to retune sort guardbands per lot and safely pass dies currently rejected by worst-case margins.
why: Yield: ~3-8% more passing dies, with less over-test time.

title: Intermediary: mature logic foundries make gain-cell DRAM with one implant mask
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: 28-40 nm logic foundries become intermediate DRAM suppliers by building standard 3T silicon gain cells from existing logic masks plus exactly one added mask that counter-dopes the write transistor to a high-Vt, low-leakage flavour.
why: Capacity: taps idle mature-node fabs (incl. U.S.) for cache/buffer-class DRAM; one mask raises retention ~10x vs. stock logic gain cells.

title: Self-service: one-mask antifuse bank lets DRAM self-repair in the field
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: one added mask defines a thick-oxide antifuse block sized for ~1% spare rows; an on-die BIST remaps weak rows during idle time, so dies keep healing through first and second lives.
why: Supply via longevity: extends module life and enables certified second-life resale, plus relaxes outgoing test.

title: Copying: convert idle NAND fabs to capacitorless DRAM with one mask
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: copy the NAND vertical-string flow and its tools wholesale, adding one mask that cuts each vertical channel into isolated floating-body segments operated as capacitorless gain-by-body-charge DRAM cells.
why: Supply: NAND overcapacity cycles become DRAM capacity; 3D density without new capacitor tooling (fact 2).

title: Cheap substitute: panel-level DRAM on idle display-glass TFT lines
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap objects: replace costly silicon wafers with 5.5 m^2 Gen-8.5 glass panels from idle display fabs, using the standard oxide-TFT backplane flow plus one added mask for a high-k storage capacitor, to make bulk low-speed capacity-tier DRAM.
why: Cost and capital: ~tens of GB per panel on fully depreciated lines; trades density for vast idle area.

title: Mechanics substitution: maskless multi-beam write for the single added layer
idea: TRIZ #28 Replace mechanical system: the one permitted extra litho layer is written by multi-beam e-beam direct write instead of a physical photomask, letting micro-fabs personalize DRAM (repair, config, customer ID) per wafer with no mask shop.
why: Capital: removes ~$1-3M mask cost and mask-shop lead time for small-volume DRAM fabs.

title: Hydraulics: fluidic self-assembly of DRAM dielets into one-mask receptor wells
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics/hydraulics: small DRAM dielets from many distributed fabs are flowed in liquid over a carrier wafer whose only added mask etches shape-matched receptor wells, where they self-seat by capillary and gravity before a common RDL.
why: Distributed manufacturing: aggregates dielets from heterogeneous sources into large modules cheaply; tiny dies yield better.

title: Thin films: porous-silicon release layer enables 10x substrate reuse
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells/thin films: one added mask defines anodization windows that form a buried porous-Si cleave plane; after array processing the thin device layer is bonded to a cheap carrier and lifted off, and the CZ wafer is re-polished and reused ~10 times.
why: Scarce resources: cuts prime-wafer and HPQ crucible demand per bit sharply.

title: Porous materials: anodized macroporous capacitors in legacy 200 mm fabs
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: one mask opens a lattice of seeds and electrochemical anodization grows deep macropores (AR >100:1) for storage capacitors, letting legacy fabs without advanced high-AR plasma etchers produce DRAM.
why: Tool chokepoint and capacitor wall (fact 1): reaches high AR with a wet bath instead of a $10M+ etcher.

title: Color change: one-mask optical grating ID enables automated reclaim grading
idea: TRIZ #32 Color change: one mask patterns a diffractive grating code in the top metal readable through the package by IR spectroscopy, carrying lot, bin and retention data so reclaimed dies are auto-sorted and priced without retest.
why: Reuse market friction: cheap trusted provenance lifts reclaimed DRAM yields and buyer confidence.

title: Homogeneity: deep-trench eDRAM built into passive silicon interposers
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: silicon interposers already made at 65 nm on plentiful lines get one added deep-trench capacitor mask (plus existing transistor flow where available) to carry GB-scale eDRAM in otherwise passive silicon under the accelerator.
why: Supply and data movement: moves some HBM demand onto under-used interposer capacity with short wires.

title: Discarding and recovering: one RDL mask stitches good dies into wafer-scale slabs
idea: TRIZ #34 Discard and recover: after wafer sort, a single per-lot RDL mask routes across scribe lines to connect only good neighbouring dies into wafer-scale memory slabs, discarding bad dies in place without dicing.
why: Packaging cost and yield: removes dicing, substrates and per-die packaging for memory appliances.

title: Parameter change: chilled-grade DRAM with one-mask on-die thermistor guarantee
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: dies failing retention at 85 C but passing at 45 C ship as 'chilled grade' for liquid-cooled racks; one added mask adds a thin-film thermistor so the controller enforces the operating window and doubles refresh if exceeded.
why: Retention yield: leakage roughly halves per ~10 C, recovering a slice of dies scrapped today.

title: Phase transition: reworkable HBM via one-mask low-melt sacrificial bond layer
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: one mask defines a low-melting indium/thermoplastic sacrificial ring at each core-die interface so a stack with a failing layer can be locally reheated, split and re-stacked with a good die.
why: HBM yield loss 20-30%: rework recovers most stacks instead of scrapping 11 good dies.

title: Thermal expansion: one-mask stressor liner lets legacy fabs hit modern speed bins
idea: TRIZ #37 Thermal expansion: one mask selectively places a high-CTE-mismatch nitride liner over periphery transistors, where cooling locks in strain that lifts drive current ~15-25% so depreciated 1x nm fabs ship faster bins.
why: Cost per bit: extends earning life of depreciated fabs instead of forcing node migration.

title: Strong oxidants: ozone leaching recovers tungsten from fab waste streams
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: ozone/peroxide oxidative leaching recovers tungsten from CVD-W chamber cleans, CMP slurry and scrap wafers as tungstate, refined back to WF6 on-site; no lithography mask is added at all.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): closes part of the loop for buried wordlines and contacts.

title: Inert atmosphere: sealed-pod minimal-fab makes DRAM inside ordinary warehouses
idea: TRIZ #39 Inert atmosphere: every wafer stays in nitrogen-filled pods docked to sealed tool minienvironments, so a fixed legacy DRAM flow plus at most one new mask runs in a standard warehouse without a ballroom cleanroom.
why: Capital and distributed U.S. manufacturing: cleanroom building cost falls by most of its share.

title: Composite: new-die cache fronts reclaimed DDR4 dies on CXL modules
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite: a CXL module pairs one new DDR5 die as a write-back cache with seven reclaimed DDR4 dies, run by an existing controller re-spun with one changed metal mask to add the caching and wear map.
why: Supply: converts recycled dies into near-new performance capacity, cutting fresh-bit demand ~85% per module.

title: Segmentation: multi-project DRAM shuttle with one custom mask per startup
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation applied to the reticle: a DRAM foundry runs a frozen base flow and splits one reticle among many startups, each allowed exactly one custom mask layer to test new cell, capacitor or array ideas.
why: Innovation throughput: ~100x cheaper experiments for new DRAM entrants than private lots.

title: Nesting: oxide-TFT memory nested in logic BEOL reusing existing masks
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: a memory layer is nested between two existing logic metal levels, reusing the via mask as the TFT gate contact and metal mask as source/drain, so the only new mask defines the oxide channel island.
why: Capacity: every logic wafer gains a memory layer for buffers, with one mask of added cost.

title: Inversion: mask-frozen DRAM nodes depreciated over 15 years
idea: TRIZ #13 Inversion: stop node migration; freeze a DRAM node's mask set for 15 years and allow just one added mask per generation for incremental gains (e.g., a second capacitor tier), so tools fully depreciate before replacement.
why: Depreciation ~55% of wafer cost: stretching tool life from 5 to 15 years cuts cost per bit more than a node shrink's 10-20%.

title: Prior action: central EUV hub ships pre-patterned wafers to one-mask spokes
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: a single EUV-equipped hub performs all critical array patterning, then ships wafers to distributed U.S. spoke fabs that finish deposition, implants and BEOL using DUV plus exactly one customization mask.
why: EUV single-supplier chokepoint: concentrates EUV use while multiplying finishing capacity cheaply.

title: Another dimension: embedded-die PCB DIMMs doubling module density
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: bare DRAM dies are embedded inside the module PCB core and connected with one added laser/litho via layer, while the surfaces carry more packaged dies, doubling GB per DIMM slot.
why: Slot-limited server capacity: more memory per socket without new dies or a new die node.

title: Asymmetry: one-mask asymmetric halo implant shrinks access-transistor leakage tail
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: one added implant mask places a halo only on the bitline side of the access transistor, keeping the storage-node junction graded and lowering GIDL, so far fewer dies fail the 13 fA retention tail.
why: Retention yield and refresh (fact 3): more passing dies per wafer and longer refresh intervals.
